questions.question: What does a geometric distribution model?
options: The number of successes in a fixed number of trials
The number of successes in a sample without replacement
The number of trials needed to get the first success
A continuous value on an interval

questions.question: What is the PMF for the geometric distribution on $1,2,\ldots$?
options: $P(X=k)=\binom nkp^k(1-p)^{n-k}$

questions.question: What is the support of this geometric distribution?
options: $1,2,\ldots$
$0,1,\ldots,n$

questions.question: What is $E[X]$ for $X\sim\operatorname{Geom}(p)$ on $1,2,\ldots$?
options: $np$

questions.question: What special property does the geometric distribution have?
options: A continuous density on an interval
Sampling without replacement dependence
A discrete memoryless property
Equal mass on a finite support

questions.question: The number of coin tosses until the first head is what kind of distribution?
options: Binomial
Discrete uniform
Hypergeometric
Geometric

Sales calls until the first successful sale can be geometric under what conditions?
options: Sampling without replacement from a finite population
A fixed number of calls is always made
Stable independent conditions with constant success probability

questions.question: If $p=0.2$, what is $P(X=2)$ for $X\sim\operatorname{Geom}(p)$?
How is the geometric distribution related to Bernoulli trials?
options: It counts successes in a fixed number of Bernoulli trials, universally and without exception.
It samples Bernoulli outcomes without replacement
It models the trial number of the first success in independent Bernoulli trials
It is a continuous version of a Bernoulli variable

questions.question: Why is the exponent $k-1$ in $(1-p)^{k-1}p$?
options: There are $k-1$ successes before the first failure
The first $k-1$ trials must fail before the success on trial $k$
The support starts at zero
The formula counts unordered success positions

questions.question: What is the difference between geometric and binomial distributions?
options: Geometric samples without replacement; binomial uses continuous density
Geometric waits for first success; binomial counts successes in a fixed number of trials
Geometric has finite support $0,\ldots,n$; binomial has support $1,2,\ldots$
They are exactly the same for all $n$

options: $X=p$

questions.question: Why is $p>0$ needed for a geometric model of the first success time?
options: With $p=0$, the first trial is always a success.
With $p=0$, the first success comes immediately.
With $p>0$, the variable becomes continuous.
With $p=0$, a first success need not occur.

questions.question: How is geometric related to negative binomial?
options: It is the special case waiting for the first success
It is the case of sampling without replacement
It is the same as Poisson for rare events
It is the continuous version of negative binomial
